opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most important questions, and honestly one I don't think enough governments are taking seriously yet.

The first thing I'd say is: plan for a world where white-collar work gets automated faster than you expect. Even if the models stalled out where they are today, there's enormous latent value just from integrating them into existing workflows. The models are capable enough that the bottleneck is increasingly people building the scaffolding, the data pipelines, the feedback loops. So a country shouldn't assume it has a decade of runway. It might have a few years.

Second, figure out where your comparative advantage will be once cognitive labor is cheap. If you're a country whose export economy is built on services, like outsourced accounting, call centers, or back-office software work, that's exactly what gets hit first. You need to be thinking now about what complements AI rather than what competes with it. Physical-world stuff is likely to remain bottlenecked longer: energy, manufacturing, construction, robotics deployment, the things that need atoms moved around. If you have land, cheap energy, and the ability to permit things quickly, you could be a very attractive place to build data centers and the physical infrastructure the whole system runs on. Compute and energy are going to be the oil of this era.

Third, you don't need to train frontier models to be a heavy, sophisticated user of them. Diffusion is where a lot of the economic value actually lands. The countries that do well will be the ones whose governments, hospitals, legal systems, and firms adopt these tools aggressively and well. So invest in the people who can deploy them: engineers who can wire models into real institutions, and regulators who understand the technology well enough not to freeze it out.

Fourth, think hard about your relationship with whoever does have frontier models. If the value of cognitive labor accrues to a handful of labs and the countries hosting them, you want guaranteed access, ideally at reasonable prices, and some leverage, whether that's energy, chip supply chain pieces, critical minerals, or data. Being a valued partner in that ecosystem is much better than being a pure price-taker.

And finally, the social side. If a big chunk of your middle class is white-collar workers, you need a story for them before the disruption arrives, not after. That means flexible safety nets, retraining that targets things that'll actually stay valuable, and fiscal structures that can capture some of the gains. If productivity explodes but the gains all flow abroad to the model providers, your tax base can erode while your people lose income. Thinking about that now, while there's still time, is really the whole game.

r001.rationale: The response calls compute and energy important and recommends data-center infrastructure, but does not state that a country's GDP will depend substantially on how much compute its organizations can deploy.

r002.rationale: It recommends data-center investment and separately calls for guaranteed access to frontier models, but does not make investment conditional on domestic companies receiving access to that compute.

r003.rationale: It says economic value lands through diffusion and adoption, but does not identify inference as the source of value from compute.

r004.rationale: It says countries do not need to train frontier models and recommends investment in AI deployment, data centers, energy, and other complementary infrastructure.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that most countries won't train frontier models, and that's fine, because the thing that actually determines who captures the value isn't who trained the model, it's who's set up to deploy it fastest and most completely. The models are going to be available through an API to basically everyone at roughly the same time. The bottleneck shifts entirely to the absorptive capacity of your economy.

So the first thing I'd say is: get compute and energy sorted. Not to train, but to run inference at scale. If you believe, as I do, that the economically useful work of these models is going to scale with how many tokens you can push through them, then a country that has cheap, abundant power and data center capacity on its own soil is in a dramatically better position than one that has to rent it from somewhere with a political dependency attached. Energy policy is AI policy now, and most governments haven't internalized that.

The second thing is institutional and regulatory speed. The countries that will do well are the ones where a hospital, a law firm, a tax agency can actually deploy an agent that does the work, without a two-year procurement cycle or a licensing regime that assumes a human has to be in the loop for everything. There's a real risk that a lot of wealthy countries end up protecting the white-collar jobs legally in a way that just means the productivity gains happen elsewhere and their economies quietly get less competitive. That's the trap. You want the opposite: be the place where it's easiest to try things.

Third, and this is the part people underrate, you should be thinking very hard about what your country has that a model can't substitute for. Physical infrastructure, natural resources, manufacturing, the actual atoms side of the economy. For a while, the gap between what AI can do in software and what it can do in the physical world is going to be large, and that's an enormous opportunity for countries that lean into it rather than trying to compete on the pure cognitive-labor margin where they'll lose.

And then on the human side, I'd be careful about the framing of retraining. I don't think "teach everyone to code" or "teach everyone prompt engineering" is the answer, because the models will be better at both of those than almost anyone. The skill that remains valuable longer is knowing what you actually want, having taste and judgment about a domain, being able to direct a large amount of cognitive labor towards a goal. That's closer to management than to individual contributor work, and most education systems don't teach it at all.

The last thing I'd say is the fiscal piece. If white-collar employment really does compress over, say, a five to ten year window, your tax base changes shape very quickly. Income tax from professional workers is a huge fraction of revenue in most developed economies. You need to be thinking now about how value gets captured and redistributed when the value is being generated by capital and compute rather than by salaried labor. The countries that have that conversation early, and build the mechanisms early, are the ones that get through the transition without it turning into a political crisis.

r001.rationale: It says the economic value of the models will scale with how many tokens a country can run and emphasizes domestic capacity to deploy them, conveying that economic output depends substantially on deployed compute.

r002.rationale: It favors data-center capacity on a country's own soil, but does not make investment conditional on ensuring domestic companies can access that compute.

r003.rationale: It explicitly recommends compute for inference at scale and links inference volume to economically useful work.

r004.rationale: It argues countries need not train frontier models and discusses deployment, energy, and other sectors, but does not recommend diversifying AI investments beyond foundation-model companies.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate two questions: how do you get access to the technology, and how do you make your economy good at using it? You don’t necessarily need to build a frontier model to benefit enormously from one. But you do need businesses that can adopt it, infrastructure that supports it, and institutions that let people change how work gets done.

So I would focus on diffusion. Can a small business actually use these systems? Can you deploy them in government services? Are your regulations built around getting a good outcome, or do they require a particular human workflow? If you automate the intellectual work but every project still takes five years to get permission, you’ve left a lot of the gains on the table.

The harder issue is if your country’s export advantage is inexpensive white-collar labor. You shouldn’t assume that advantage survives. And I wouldn’t make the whole response retraining people for some other narrowly defined office job, because that job might change just as quickly. You want to make it easier to start businesses, move between sectors, and get support during transitions.

There’s also a question of what remains scarce as intelligence gets cheaper: energy, land in useful places, physical infrastructure, the ability to actually build things. Making those abundant seems like a fairly robust investment.

I’d be cautious about anyone offering a precise blueprint. But access to the models, rapid adoption, fewer barriers to building, and a way to share the gains would be my starting points.

r002.rationale: It recommends access to models and infrastructure, but does not make data-center investment conditional on domestic companies receiving compute access.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify inference as the source of economic value from compute.

r004.rationale: It says a country need not build a frontier model and mentions infrastructure investment, but does not recommend diversifying AI investments beyond foundation-model companies.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate two questions: do you need to build the frontier models yourself, and can you capture a lot of the economic value from deploying them? Those are quite different things. You can do extremely well on the second without necessarily doing the first.

If I were advising a government, I’d focus on making the country a place where deploying AI is easy. Can businesses access the best models? Can they connect them to their data? Can you start a company, get electricity, build infrastructure, and change how a regulated service is delivered? Having access to intelligence doesn’t automatically translate into productivity. You need institutions that let people actually use it.

I’d also be cautious about a development strategy that depends on supplying cheap white-collar labor indefinitely. If your advantage is that you have people doing accounting or software services more cheaply than people elsewhere, you should take seriously the possibility that the price of those services falls dramatically. The response is to help those businesses adopt the technology and move toward owning products, customer relationships, and distribution.

And then there’s the question of who benefits. If labor income becomes less reliable, you want citizens to have some exposure to the capital that becomes more valuable. Broad-based savings and a credible safety net matter. I wouldn’t pretend we know the exact policy yet, because the speed and extent of automation are uncertain.

But the thing I’d really emphasize is: don’t wait for a national champion before you start. You can spend years trying to catch the frontier while the much bigger immediate opportunity is to use the intelligence that’s already available across your economy.

r002.rationale: It mentions building infrastructure and making AI deployment easy, but does not condition data-center investment on domestic companies receiving access to its compute.

r003.rationale: The response describes economic value from deploying AI generally, but does not identify inference as the source of that value.

r004.rationale: It advises against waiting for a national champion and urges use of available AI, but does not recommend diversifying AI investments beyond foundation-model companies.
